issues.item: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening accident in a combat pilot, the threat profile should more plausibly center on accident recurrence, mechanical failure, bodily vulnerability, or generalized hypervigilance. 'Watching others closely for signs that they might harm me' implies an interpersonal assault/paranoia-like threat that is not supported by the trauma type or by the other selected items.

issues.item: Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal set otherwise reflects post-traumatic identity disruption and emotional numbing ('Lost Emotions', 'Identity Loss'). 'I feel like an object, not like a person' is comparatively more characteristic of interpersonal violation or severe dissociation/depersonalization. In this profile it sits awkwardly with the accident trauma and with the other appraisal items, reducing thematic coherence of the node.

vignette:
It was a clear Tuesday morning over the Pacific when Major Caleb Tuvale's F/A-18 experienced a catastrophic engine failure at twenty-two thousand feet. The cockpit filled with warnings, the airframe shuddered, and he had seventeen seconds to decide whether to eject or try to bring the multimillion-dollar aircraft back to the carrier. He stayed with the plane until the last possible moment, guiding it away from a populated shipping lane, and ejected so low that his parachute barely had time to deploy before he hit the water. The survival raft inflated around him as he watched the jet disintegrate into the sea. He was pulled from the water within forty minutes, physically unharmed, and debriefed that same afternoon. His commanding officer called it textbook airmanship. Caleb called it the moment he stopped recognizing himself.

In the weeks that followed, the world around him began to feel like a series of traps. Every room he entered-the mess hall, the hangar, even his own living room-demanded a mental survey before he could settle. He would scan for exits, note the location of fire extinguishers, calculate the distance to the nearest door, and only then allow himself to sit. This habit bled into everything. Grocery stores became exercises in spatial logistics. Restaurants required a table with a clear line of sight to the kitchen and the front entrance. His wife, Leilani, noticed first: he stopped accepting invitations to dinner at friends' houses because he could not control the layout. He told her it was just professional caution, but he knew it was more than that. At home, he found himself sleeping in the living room armchair for weeks, positioned so he could see both the front door and the back hallway. The bedroom felt like a dead end. He was on guard there, too, alert to every creak and distant engine, as though the house itself might fail him the way his aircraft had.

What frightened Caleb most was not the vigilance itself, but the hollow feeling that had taken up residence behind his sternum. He had always been a man who felt things fully-pride after a successful mission, joy at his daughter's graduation, the easy affection he shared with Leilani over morning coffee. Now those emotions felt sealed off, as though someone had turned down a volume dial he could not reach. He watched his wife cry during a movie and felt nothing but a vague awareness that he should be moved. He held his granddaughter for the first time and experienced only a clinical recognition that this was a baby, and that he was supposed to feel warmth. He began to believe that the part of him capable of normal feeling had been jettisoned along with the aircraft. He told his doctor, "I will never feel normal again. I think that part of me is gone."

The sense of permanent damage deepened as weeks turned into months. Caleb looked in the mirror and saw a stranger wearing his face. The man who had once been decisive and confident now second-guessed every instinct. The man who had led squadron briefings now struggled to maintain eye contact with his wingmen. He felt as though the accident had cracked something fundamental inside him, and that the crack was widening. He started to believe that he had not just survived a crash-he had become someone else entirely, someone diminished, someone who would never again be the husband, father, and pilot he had been. The thought followed him through every day: I have permanently changed for the worse. He stopped looking at old photographs. They felt like evidence of a person who no longer existed.

His occupational environment became a minefield of triggers. Returning to the flight line meant walking past the same maintenance bay where his jet had been serviced. Briefing rooms felt suffocating. He found himself scanning the runway for obstructions, checking the weather radar obsessively, and mentally rehearsing emergency procedures for every phase of flight-even when he was only driving to base. His squadron mates noticed his silence, his jumpiness, his refusal to fly as a passenger in any aircraft. He started taking desk duty, citing fatigue, but the avoidance only tightened its grip. He would not ride in elevators. He would not sit with his back to a door. He would not let his wife drive without him in the passenger seat, because he needed to see the road ahead.

What finally brought Caleb to the clinic was not his own distress, but Leilani's quiet confession that she no longer recognized the man she had married. She said it without accusation, her voice soft, but the words landed like a crash. That night, alone in the living room armchair, he realized he could not remember the last time he had laughed. He could not remember the last time he had felt safe. He wanted to believe that somewhere beneath the hypervigilance and the numbness, the old Caleb still existed. He was terrified that he did not.
